title: The Anglo-Saxons arrive
blurb: Bede's traditional date for the coming of Angles, Saxons and Jutes across the North Sea. Their Germanic dialects become Old English, and the Celtic languages of Britain retreat west and north.

title: Augustine lands in Kent
blurb: Pope Gregory's missionaries bring Roman Christianity — and Latin church words like altar, candle, school and monk.

title: Cædmon's Hymn
blurb: Bede tells of Cædmon, a herdsman at Whitby Abbey who began to sing of the Creation in English — the earliest English poem by a poet we can name.

title: Vikings sack Lindisfarne
blurb: Norse raiders attack the monastery of Lindisfarne in June 793. Within a century raiding has turned to settlement.

title: Alfred and the Danelaw
blurb: Alfred the Great defeats the Danish leader Guthrum at Edington; the peace that follows leaves the north and east under Danish rule — the Danelaw — where Norse and English mingle into words like they, egg, sky and law.

title: The Beowulf manuscript
blurb: Around the year 1000 two scribes copy Beowulf, the longest surviving Old English poem, into the book now kept in the British Library.

title: The Norman Conquest
blurb: William of Normandy wins at Hastings on 14 October. For some three centuries England's rulers speak French, while English lives on in the fields and kitchens.

title: Normandy is lost
blurb: King John loses Normandy to the French crown, and England's nobles slowly come to see themselves as English. French words keep arriving — now more often from Paris than from Normandy.

title: A proclamation in English
blurb: Henry III's proclamation of the Provisions of Oxford is issued in English as well as French and Latin — the first royal proclamation in English since the Conquest.

title: English in the courts
blurb: The Statute of Pleading orders that lawsuits be argued in English, since French was ‘much unknown’ — though the statute itself is written in French. The same year, Parliament is opened with a speech in English.

title: The Canterbury Tales
blurb: Geoffrey Chaucer writes his pilgrims' tales in the English of London, rich with French borrowings, and shows that English can carry great literature.

title: The Great Vowel Shift begins
blurb: Over roughly three centuries the long vowels of English move: ‘mees’ becomes mice and ‘hoos’ becomes house. Spelling, settled by printers mid-shift, still records many of the old sounds.

title: Caxton's printing press
blurb: William Caxton sets up the first printing press in England, at Westminster. Printed books spread the London dialect and begin to fix spelling.

title: Tyndale's New Testament
blurb: William Tyndale's English New Testament, printed abroad, is smuggled into England. He later coins scapegoat and Passover, and much of his wording lives on in the King James Bible.

title: The inkhorn controversy
blurb: Thomas Wilson's Arte of Rhetorique mocks ‘inkhorn terms’ — showy Latin coinages. Thousands of Latin and Greek words pour in anyway; many stick, many vanish.

title: Shakespeare's plays
blurb: Shakespeare, born in 1564, writes his plays in London from about 1590 to 1613. He is the first recorded user of hundreds of words, from bedroom to lonely, though many were surely already in speech.

title: The East India Company
blurb: Chartered on 31 December 1600, the Company opens two centuries of trade and then empire in Asia, bringing home words like bungalow, pyjamas, shampoo and loot.

title: The first English dictionary
blurb: Robert Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall explains about 2,500 ‘hard usual English words’ borrowed from Latin, Greek and French — the first dictionary of English in English.

title: Jamestown
blurb: The first permanent English settlement in America is founded in Virginia. Powhatan and other Algonquian languages soon give English raccoon, moccasin and tomahawk.

title: The King James Bible
blurb: Read aloud in churches for centuries, its cadences and phrases — ‘the salt of the earth’, ‘a law unto themselves’ — sink deep into the language.

title: Johnson's Dictionary
blurb: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language defines some 42,000 words, illustrated with quotations from great writers — and a few jokes, like ‘lexicographer: a harmless drudge’.

title: American independence
blurb: The Declaration of Independence launches a nation whose English will diverge from Britain's, and eventually lead it — from OK to cyberspace.

title: The First Fleet reaches Australia
blurb: British ships arrive at Sydney Cove in January 1788. Aboriginal languages give English boomerang, koala and wombat, and Australian English begins.

title: Webster's American Dictionary
blurb: Noah Webster's American Dictionary of the English Language spreads American spellings like color, center and theater.

title: A new dictionary is proposed
blurb: Richard Chenevix Trench's papers to the Philological Society call for a dictionary recording every English word and its history — the project that becomes the Oxford English Dictionary.

title: The OED's first instalment
blurb: The first fascicle of the Oxford English Dictionary, A to Ant, appears under its editor James Murray. The whole first edition is finished only in 1928.

title: BBC radio
blurb: The British Broadcasting Company begins regular broadcasts in November 1922, carrying a standard accent into millions of homes.

title: English goes global
blurb: After the Second World War, American power, science, film and trade make English the world's leading second language — and a lender of words to almost every other.

title: ARPANET
blurb: On 29 October 1969 the first message passes between networked computers in California. It was meant to be LOGIN; the system crashed after LO.

title: The World Wide Web
blurb: Tim Berners-Lee's Web opens to the public in August 1991, and online life becomes a word factory: blog, spam, google, meme.

title: Social media
blurb: Facebook launches in February 2004, soon followed by YouTube and Twitter. Words like unfriend, hashtag and selfie spread worldwide in months.

title: ‘Selfie’ is Word of the Year
blurb: Oxford Dictionaries crowns selfie, first spotted on an Australian forum in 2002, after its use grew some 17,000% in a single year.

title: AI chatbots
blurb: ChatGPT's release in November 2022 puts conversational AI in millions of hands; Collins names AI its Word of the Year for 2023.
